verses.1: Al-Mizan: a disbeliever's demanded punishment is inevitable, comes from Allah, Lord of the Stairways, and cannot be averted.
verses.2: Al-Mizan: a disbeliever's demanded punishment is inevitable, comes from Allah, Lord of the Stairways, and cannot be averted.
verses.3: Al-Mizan allows "from Allah" to qualify either the punishment or the impossibility of deflecting it. Maʿārij are real, existential stations of proximity in the malakūt through which angels and the Spirit ascend; the ascent of true belief and righteous deeds, and believers' ranks, reduce to this primary meaning rather than merely mental or social positions. The fifty-thousand-year day is the Resurrection, projected into worldly time: as causal intermediaries disappear, angels return to their stations around the Throne. The unqualified al-rūḥ is a being of the divine command distinct from angels, not Gabriel, whose titles are qualified. Graceful patience excludes fret, complaint, and agitation. The rejectors' seeing the punishment or Day as remote means treating it as impossible, whereas God's knowledge makes it near and grounds the Prophet's patience. Kal-muhl is molten metal, marking the time of the inevitable punishment.
verses.4: The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him on a day of fifty thousand years.
verses.6: They see it as far off, but God sees it near.
verses.7: They see it as far off, but God sees it near.
verses.8: Al-Mizan describes the Day: the sky becomes molten copper and mountains carded wool; friends are shown one another but do not inquire, while the guilty would ransom themselves with their children, spouse, brother, kin, and all people on earth to escape punishment.
verses.9: Al-Mizan reads ʿihn as wool, perhaps specifically carded wool. It reports red wool and dyed wool as alternatives, the latter linked to mountains' different colors.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains ḥamīm as a caring close friend or relative, yet on the Resurrection everyone is too consumed by personal distress to ask after such friends. Yubaṣṣarūnahum means that these friends and relatives are shown one another; it independently answers the implied question whether they see each other, though it may also qualify "friend." Readings that show angels to disbelievers, comfort believers by displaying punished opponents, or show leaders to those they misled lack evidence. The guilty person's desire, yawaddu, is to ransom himself through children, spouse, brother, faṣīlah—his closest sheltered kin—and all intelligent beings on earth; his sinfulness is broader than disbelief. Kallā rejects that ransom: laẓā is an unceasing blazing fire, and nazzāʿah strips limbs. It summons those who turn from faith and worship and hoard wealth instead of giving charity to the needy and deprived.

verses.15: Ransom is refused: it is a blazing fire that strips away limbs.
verses.16: Ransom is refused: it is a blazing fire that strips away limbs.
verses.17: Al-Mizan's introduction says the sūrah describes Resurrection, inevitable punishment for disbelievers, and the exception of believers with true belief and obligatory good deeds. Although conventionally called Meccan, it argues from the contextual unity of the verses on zakāt, the Medinan hypocrites, and the response to (8:32) that the whole sūrah was revealed in Medina; a narration from Imām al-Ṣādiq makes the "known right" voluntary rather than obligatory zakāt, but consensus and an Ibn ʿAbbās dating report cannot override this evidence. In the exposition of (70:1) and (70:2), suʾāl is a defiant demand, not an inquiry: bāʾ can express deliberate attention or emphasis but not mean ʿan. The inevitable punishment will strike the disbelievers with no deflector, making the response to their demand derisive. Hell calls those who turn from the divine summons and hoard wealth rather than give the needy their due; its unextinguished blaze strips limbs, and it makes ransom impossible.

verses.19: Al-Mizan describes the human as covetous—fretful in hardship and grudging in prosperity—except those marked by prayer, a known right in their wealth for the beggar and deprived, practical affirmation of requital, apprehension of their Lord’s punishment, sexual restraint within the stated bounds, fidelity to trusts and covenants, truthful testimony, and watchfulness over prayer.

verses.21: Al-Mizan describes the human as covetous—fretful in hardship and grudging in prosperity—except those marked by prayer, a known right in their wealth for the beggar and deprived, practical affirmation of requital, apprehension of their Lord’s punishment, sexual restraint within the stated bounds, fidelity to trusts and covenants, truthful testimony, and watchfulness over prayer.
verses.22: Al-Mizan takes the exception from the covetous ‘man.’ Prayer is named first to show its rank as the best deed and its significant role in restraining covetousness (29:45).
verses.23: Al-Mizan takes ‘their prayer’ to mean steadfast observance at its due times, not unceasing physical performance. A deed bears its full fruit only through such persistence.
verses.24: Al-Mizan distinguishes the sāʾil, a needy person who asks, from the maḥrūm, a needy person who honourably refrains from asking. Although some exegetes identify the known right with obligatory zakāt, a narration from Imam al-Ṣādiq identifies it as a known share voluntarily set aside for the poor. The commentary finds support in the verse’s apparent limitation to these two recipients, unlike the wider classes entitled to zakāt in (9:60).

verses.26: Al-Mizan understands yuṣaddiqūna as practical, not merely intellectual, affirmation of the Day of Retribution: their lives show persistent awareness that good and evil will be repaid. The present tense conveys their continuing mindfulness of God, fulfilling what pleases Him and avoiding what He disapproves.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan equates mushfiqūn with khāʾifūn and reads their fear as practical awe visible in conduct. Even with good deeds, they do not trust their own righteousness or feel secure from punishment, since punishment follows disobedience and a servant controls nothing except by God’s authorization.

Though God promises deliverance to obedient servants and does not break His promise, the promise does not limit His omnipotence so that He could no longer act otherwise. The commentary therefore holds that one must remain awed by His absolute power; it notes that angels and prophets are described as fearing Him, while these believers are still affirmed to be honoured in gardens (70:35).
verses.28: Al-Mizan says the verse justifies the believers’ apprehension: fear of their Lord’s punishment is warranted for the reasons already given.
verses.29: Al-Mizan refers the exposition of this restriction on sexual relations and its transgression to its commentary on the opening verses of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn (23:5-7).
verses.30: Al-Mizan refers the exposition of this restriction on sexual relations and its transgression to its commentary on the opening verses of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn (23:5-7).
verses.31: Al-Mizan refers the exposition of this restriction on sexual relations and its transgression to its commentary on the opening verses of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn (23:5-7).
verses.32:
Al-Mizan first understands trusts as entrusted property and matters placed in another’s care, such as dependents and reputation; keeping them means protecting them from breach. It reports broader readings that include every obligatory belief and act, hence both God’s and people’s rights, or every divine blessing, whose misuse breaches a divine trust.

The commentary apparently takes covenant (ʿahd) as any verbal or practical contract, kept by abiding by it and not violating it. It also reports that covenant can include every commitment, including faith in God, so disobeying His injunctions breaches that covenant.
verses.33: Al-Mizan defines shahādah as testimony and says standing by it requires neither withholding it when called upon nor concealing or distorting the facts.
verses.34: Al-Mizan says watchfulness over prayer is preserving the prayer’s recommended and legally prescribed qualities. It distinguishes this from constancy in prayer: the latter concerns performing the act itself, while the former concerns its manner and quality. The ‘they’ who are honoured are those introduced as praying; the indefinite gardens magnify them. The verse can mean that they have both gardens and honour, or that they are honoured within the gardens.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan identifies halaʿ as intense covetousness: an inborn, self-regarding desire for what one judges personally good, rather than indiscriminate greed. Fretfulness before misfortune and possessiveness at fortune are its consequences. As a branch of self-love, it is originally a means to happiness and perfection, not a vice; like other psychological qualities, it is virtuous when properly directed and moderated, and vicious when pursued without propriety or fairness.

The commentary traces its unrestrained form from the infant appetite, which meets pain with agitation and competes for apparent goods, to the mature person's ability through reason to distinguish truth from falsehood and real good from bad. Persisting in desire, falsehood, and violations of others’ rights seals the heart unless divine grace redirects desire toward truth and each person’s due. Reason can instead direct this self-interest toward alarm at sin, eagerness for forgiveness and lasting blessing, and patience in calamity, obedience, and against disobedience. Rejecting reason and fiṭrah turns God’s blessing into damnation, expressed in forsaking truth and hoarding wealth.

Al-Mizan therefore attributes the quality to human creation while locating the condemnation in human misuse, not in God’s act. It rejects al-Zamakhsharī’s figurative account that people are only described as if created with the trait because rebuke and the believers’ exception rule out its being innate: believers retain the inherent quality in its sound state rather than lack it. It also rejects the proposed unconnected exception.
verses.36: Al-Mizan questions why the disbelievers assemble around the Prophet with hostile stares in scattered groups from right and left.
verses.37: Al-Mizan questions why the disbelievers assemble around the Prophet with hostile stares in scattered groups from right and left.
verses.38: They cannot expect admission to the Garden of Bliss.
verses.39: They were created from what they know.
verses.40: Al-Mizan affirms that the Lord of the easts and wests can replace them with better people, and none can outmaneuver Him.
verses.41: Al-Mizan affirms that the Lord of the easts and wests can replace them with better people, and none can outmaneuver Him.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan frames these verses as the final answer to disbelievers who gather around the Prophet, looking at him from scattered sides while aspiring to paradise. Qibal denotes the direction one faces; muhṭiʿīn can denote hostile fixed gazes or rushing, and ʿizīn scattered groups. The initial fāʾ is fāʾ al-faṣīḥah, making explicit the implication of the preceding contrast: only the righteous believers are destined for honour, so why should disbelievers hope to evade that decree?

The shift from their collective staring to each person’s hope shows that salvation requires individual aspiration leading to belief and righteous deeds; group desire does not save each member. The passive yudkhala further means that entry into paradise is by God’s admission, not personal choice. Al-Mizan rejects the report that Meccan polytheists mockingly claimed precedence in paradise while denying the hereafter, because that account conflicts with the verses’ serious concern with paradise and hell. It instead identifies the audience as Medinan hypocrites: outward converts who disbelieved by rejecting some revealed commands, so proximity to the Prophet cannot profit them.

‘Never’ rejects their hope because they know they were created from semen and can be removed and replaced. The commentary rejects three alternative grammatical readings of min-mā, whether min means purpose, a starting point requiring purification, or mā denotes the rational human genus, as implausible in the text and context. The Lord of the easts and wests refers primarily to the many daily rising and setting points of the sun, possibly those of all stars; the pronoun shifts intensify God’s oath, His creative attribute across time, and the majesty of His power. Universal lordship proves that no created thing can restrain His ability to substitute a better community, for such restraint would make it a partner in lordship.

The omitted object in ‘replace’ reflects the disbelievers’ worthlessness, while the better people would believe and follow truth. The comparative ‘better’ also supports the hypocrite reading, since their outward religious profession left them some good unlike absolute polytheists. Thus continuing creation establishes that God neither must admit them to paradise nor can be defeated in reserving it for believing people of good deeds. Finally, the Prophet is told to cease exhausting himself in argument and leave them in futile khawḍ and laʿib until their promised Resurrection-day, called their day because it is when they will be punished.
verses.43: Al-Mizan identifies the promised day as the Resurrection, when people emerge from the graves rushing as though toward a signpost. It takes nuṣub as a guiding marker set on roads, rejecting ‘idol’ as unsupported by Qur’anic usage.
verses.44: Al-Mizan defines khushūʿ as the heart’s response when confronting greatness, distinguished from bodily khuḍūʿ; the eyes here display that inward humility. Rahq is a forceful covering, and dhālika gathers the preceding picture of rushing from graves, humbled eyes, and encompassing abasement into the promised day.
